justification: All human genetic evidence for CHRNA1 in this set concerns neuromuscular junction disorders — congenital myasthenic syndromes, autoimmune myasthenia gravis, and fetal akinesia/multiple pterygium syndromes (PMIDs 20562457, 20157724, 18252226, 18179903, 17687331) — none of which involve epilepsy. The only article mentioning epilepsy at all (PMID 17868079) positions CHRNA1 as a positional candidate for a porcine ataxia/spastic paresis phenotype, and the authors explicitly reject CHRNA1 (and the other candidates) as causal; this is a non-human study and a negative result. Remaining papers are zebrafish or in vitro splicing/muscle-development studies (PMIDs 15128655, 16249237, 18806275, 19147685) relevant to muscle acetylcholine receptor function, not seizure biology. A small residual weight is given to "Hypothesized" because nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits as a family have conceptual links to epileptogenesis, but the muscle alpha1 subunit has no CNS expression evidence here. There are no articles reporting CHRNA1 variants in epilepsy patients, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded.

justification: All of the provided literature concerns MYH2 (fast myosin heavy chain IIa) in the context of skeletal muscle biology and hereditary myosin myopathies — dominant E706K myopathy, recessive null mutations causing early-onset myopathy with ophthalmoplegia, muscle fiber-type regulation, and training-induced isoform shifts. None of the articles mention autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, social/behavioral outcomes, or brain expression of MYH2. There is no genetic, expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking MYH2 to ASD in this corpus; the gene's described biology (sarcomeric thick filament function) provides no logical mechanistic bridge to ASD. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a negligible allowance for an indirect biological argument.

justification: The only human autism-specific genetic evidence is a single case report of a child with autistic disorder carrying a large de novo ~19 Mb 4q32–q34 deletion that renders him hemizygous for GRIA2 along with GLRA3, GLRB, NPY1R and NPY5R (PMID 15090072); by the stated rules a multigene deletion cannot single out GRIA2 and cannot support "Established", and it also leaves the "Existing" case tentative. A related 4q32 deletion case (PMID 20358617) involves mental retardation/psychosis, not autism, and the CNV study in intellectually disabled children (PMID 19623214) merely enriches for glutamate receptor genes including GRIA2 in a non-autism cohort. Remaining support is biological: GluR2/3 AMPA receptor trafficking is disrupted by autism-associated EPAC2 mutations (PMID 19734897), and GRIA2 variation/expression studies target other phenotypes (schizophrenia, lithium response, ALS) rather than autism. Thus the evidence sits between a single suggestive human candidate-gene report ("Existing") and purely mechanistic/pathway plausibility ("Hypothesized"), with no replicated causal variant data.

Because neurexin–neuroligin synaptic adhesion pathways are strongly implicated in ASD, the biology of LRRTM2 is directly relevant, supporting a "Hypothesized" relationship rather than a genetically demonstrated one. The only disease mention for the family is LRRTM1 with schizophrenia/handedness, cited as background and not applicable to LRRTM2 or ASD. No articles report ASD-associated variants in LRRTM2 in human probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is very unlikely. A modest weight remains for Novel since autism is never explicitly addressed in the provided literature.

justification: No article in this set reports KCNC1 variants in epilepsy patients or families; the human genetic reports involving KCNC1 concern Usher syndrome 1C positional mapping (PMIDs 9445488, 9041816), where KCNC1 was screened and no mutations found, and the related KCNC3 gene is tied to SCA13 rather than epilepsy. However, substantial biological plausibility exists: Kv3.1 channels mediate fast repolarization in fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons critical for network inhibition and synchrony (PMIDs 18708127, 18775767, 12592408), the antiepileptic drug levetiracetam inhibits Kv3.1 current (PMID 20065495), and Kv3.1/Kv3.2 subunits are implicated in 4-aminopyridine-induced ictogenesis and expression changes in chronic epileptic rats (PMID 17942314). These are animal, in vitro, or heterologous expression data, supporting a mechanistic hypothesis rather than human genetic association. Therefore Hypothesized is by far the most appropriate category, with only small residual probability for Existing/Novel.
